title: The Son Before All Things
implication: ​ Sequence 1 is the Aleph standing alone — the first letter, the ox and the leader, the number of absolute unity, and the only letter in the alphabet with no sound of its own. Every other letter makes a noise; the Aleph is silence given a shape, and all sound passes through it. The year opens on the letter that carries every voice and speaks with none, and today's theme is the Son who existed before anything that could be spoken about Him. He is the One through whom all things were said into being, and He was Himself unsaid — silent, prior, and holding everything together before the first sound was made.
theme: We open the quarter where the apostles open their account of the Son — not at His birth, but before anything existed to be born into. Colossians places Him prior to creation and superior to it, and the whole of CMI's worship this quarter stands on that ground: we are not celebrating a good man who was later honoured, nor a teacher promoted after His death. We are celebrating the One through whom everything that exists was made and for whom it was made. Establish this first because everything else in the quarter depends on it. A congregation that begins with the Son's usefulness will end with a religion of benefits. A congregation that begins with His supremacy can survive a year in which the benefits are delayed.

school.title: The Image of the Invisible God
school.text: Paul does not say the Son resembles God; he says He is the image of the invisible One. Hebrews puts the same claim differently — the radiance of His glory and the exact representation of His nature (Hebrews 1:3). Teach the congregation that we do not learn what God is like from our circumstances, our upbringing or our instincts about fairness. We learn it from the Son, and where the two disagree, the Son corrects the rest.

school.title: All Things Through Him and For Him
school.text: Two prepositions carry the doctrine. Through Him — He is the agent of creation, not a product of it. For Him — creation has a purpose and the purpose is a Person. Apply it directly: a life organised around any other end is not merely unwise, it is aimed at the wrong target. Ask the congregation what their week is actually for.

school.title: In Him All Things Hold Together
school.text: The verb describes continuous sustaining, not a single act of assembly. Whatever is still standing in your life is being held. Teach this against the anxiety of the self-managed believer, who behaves as though the coherence of their world depends on their own vigilance, and who therefore cannot rest.

school.title: The Glory He Had Before
school.text: In John 17:5 the Son asks the Father to restore the glory He had with Him before the world was. He is not requesting promotion; He is requesting return. Close by showing that the humility of the incarnation is measured by the height it was a descent from (Philippians 2:5-8), and that this is the character of the One we come to the Table to receive.

communion: Open the quarter's first Table by naming who is hosting it. Say plainly to the congregation: the One who invites us to this bread is the One through whom we were made, and He is not asking us to remember a stranger.
bread: He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together. We take this bread from the hands of the Maker, who did not send someone else to be broken for what He had made.
cup: All things were created through Him and for Him — and this cup is the price He paid for the very creation that refused Him. We take it as those who belong to Him twice: by making, and by purchase.
summons: Go into this week under one Owner. Name the single area of your life where the Son currently has no operating authority, and place it under Him before you sleep tonight. Then ask of every commitment on your calendar this week: what is this actually for?

title: The Word Made Flesh
implication: Sequence 8 is the Chet standing alone — the fence and the enclosure, the letter of life, and the number that stands one beyond the completed seven and therefore beyond the natural order. The Chet is drawn as two strokes joined by a bridge across the top: two separate things roofed over into one. That is precisely the doctrine of this Sabbath. In the incarnation, what belongs beyond the natural order entered an enclosure of flesh, and two natures were bridged in one Person without either being lost.
theme: Last Sabbath we established where the Son was before. This Sabbath we follow Him into our condition. John's prologue moves in one direction only — downward — from the Word who was with God to the Word who took on flesh and pitched His tent among us. Teach the congregation to feel the scandal of it before they feel the comfort. God did not send a message about Himself; He arrived in a body that could be tired, hungry, grieved and killed.

school.title: Dwelt Among Us
school.text: John's verb describes pitching a tent rather than building a house — a provisional, portable, deliberately temporary residence. Teach what that says about the manner of God's nearness: He did not arrive in a fortress but in a form that could be moved, wounded and removed. Nearness of that kind costs the One who draws near.

school.title: Full of Grace and Truth
school.text: John names two qualities together that most people hold in tension and most churches hold in imbalance. Grace without truth produces sentiment; truth without grace produces cruelty with a verse attached. In the Son they are not blended in careful proportion — He is full of both. Ask the congregation which of the two they habitually sacrifice, and to whom.

school.title: He Has Explained Him
school.text: The word John uses is the root of our word exegesis: the Son is the exposition of the Father. Set this beside John 14:9 — he who has seen Me has seen the Father. This is the interpretive rule for all of CMI's teaching: no doctrine of God may be preached in this house that could not be preached with the Son standing in front of it.

school.title: Made Like His Brothers in All Things
school.text: Hebrews 2:14-18 gives the purpose of the incarnation in three verbs: to partake of flesh and blood, to render powerless the one who had the power of death, and to become a merciful and faithful high priest. Close on the pastoral edge of it: He is able to come to the aid of those who are tempted because He was tempted, and that is not sympathy from a distance.

communion: Introduce the Table as the continuation of the incarnation's logic. He took a body in order to give it. The elements in our hands are physical for the same reason the Word became flesh: God deals with us where we actually live.
bread: The Word became flesh. We take bread — ordinary, material, chewable — because the salvation of God did not arrive as an idea and does not sustain us as one.
cup: He shared in flesh and blood so that through death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death. We take this cup as those He was not ashamed to call brothers.
summons: This week, go where you would rather send a message. Choose one relationship you have been managing at a distance and close the distance in person. And in one conversation where you usually choose either grace or truth, carry both.

title: This Is My Beloved Son
implication: Sequence 15 carries the alphabet's most reverent convention. By plain arithmetic it would be Yod (10) and Hei (5), but those letters spell a divine Name, so fifteen is written Tet (9) and Vav (6) instead — the alphabet steps aside rather than handle the Name casually in ordinary counting. Today the Father does what the alphabet declines to do: He speaks over the Son and names Him aloud. And the letters given in the Name's place are exact — Tet, the vessel of concealed good, and Vav, the nail that fastens heaven to earth. Thirty years of hidden good are declared and fastened in a single sentence from an opened heaven.
theme: At the Jordan the Son is publicly identified by the Father before He has preached a sermon, healed anyone or gathered a disciple. The declaration precedes the ministry. That order is the single most liberating fact available to a working congregation. Teach it carefully, because almost every believer in the room has inverted it — building an identity out of output, and then defending the output because the identity depends on it.

school.title: The Declaration Before the Work
school.text: Nothing in the public ministry has yet happened. The Father is not pleased with results; He is pleased with the Son. Press the application: if the Father's pleasure in the Son preceded the Son's ministry, then our standing before God is not the wage of our usefulness.

school.title: Three Persons in One Scene
school.text: The Son in the water, the Spirit descending, the Father speaking. Teach the Trinity from the text rather than from a diagram, and note that the entire Godhead is present at the beginning of the Son's public obedience. We are never sent alone, because He was not.

school.title: Adopted Into the Same Word
school.text: Romans 8:14-17 and Galatians 4:6-7 place believers inside that declaration: we receive a spirit of adoption by which we cry Abba, Father. The word spoken over the Son at the Jordan is the word spoken over everyone in Him. Guard against sentimentality here — adoption in the ancient world was a legal act creating an irreversible claim, not a feeling of belonging.

school.title: Sons, and Therefore Heirs
school.text: Paul finishes the thought with an inheritance and a condition: heirs of God and fellow heirs with Messiah, if indeed we suffer with Him so that we may also be glorified with Him. Close honestly. The identity is a gift; the road it puts you on is not comfortable, and the congregation should know both before the Table.

communion: Bring the congregation to the Table as sons and daughters rather than as workers collecting wages. Say it directly: nothing you did this week improved your welcome here, and nothing you failed to do reduced it.
bread: This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well-pleased. We take the bread inside that sentence, for the Father's pleasure in the Son is the ground of His welcome of us.
cup: We have received a spirit of adoption. We take the cup as heirs — not applicants, not employees, not guests on probation.
summons: This week, stop auditioning. Identify the one place where you are working to secure a standing you have already been given, and deliberately do less there. Then say the Father's word over someone else: bless one person by name who has nothing to offer you.

title: The Son Who Was Tested
kicker: Fourth Sabbath — Tempted, Yet Without Sin
implication: Sequence 22 is Kaf (20) and Bet (2), and twenty-two is the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet — the complete inventory of what anything can be said with. The Kaf is the open palm, capacity, the hand that holds without dropping; the Bet is the house. On the Sabbath of the Son's testing, the sequence supplies the full complement of speech, an open hand and a dwelling — because the assault came in words, aimed at what had just been declared, and the house that withstood it was not defended by force but by an answer.
theme: Immediately after the Father's declaration, the Spirit leads the Son into the wilderness to be tempted. Note the sequence with the congregation: affirmation, then testing — and the testing is not a contradiction of the affirmation but its confirmation. Most believers interpret a hard season as evidence that something has gone wrong with their standing. The order of these two events forbids that reading.

school.title: Led By the Spirit Into the Wilderness
school.text: The wilderness was not a detour and not an ambush. He was led there. Teach the congregation to stop assuming that difficulty implies disobedience, while equally refusing the opposite error of treating every consequence of foolishness as a divine test.

school.title: Three Assaults on a Confirmed Identity
school.text: Two of the three temptations begin with the same conditional: if You are the Son of God. The attack is aimed precisely at what the Father had just declared. Show the congregation where their own testing lands — not usually on doctrine, but on identity, and always at the point of hunger, exposure or ambition.

school.title: Tempted in All Things, Yet Without Sin
school.text: Hebrews makes a claim that must be taught carefully: He did not sin, and therefore He knows the full weight of temptation rather than less of it. The one who yields discovers the pressure only up to the point of surrender. Only the one who never yielded knows how heavy it goes.

school.title: Therefore Draw Near With Confidence
school.text: Hebrews' conclusion is not caution but boldness. The result of having a tested High Priest is that we approach the throne in the moment of temptation rather than after it. Confront the instinct to withdraw from God until the crisis has passed, which is precisely backwards and is the cause of most avoidable falls.

communion: Set the Table today for people currently under pressure. Ask the congregation to come with the temptation still active rather than waiting until they feel they have mastered it — this is the throne of grace, and it exists for the time of need.
bread: He was tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin. We take the bread from One who is not disappointed to see us here in the middle of a struggle.
cup: Let us draw near with confidence. We take the cup as those who receive mercy for what has already failed and grace for what has not yet been faced.
summons: This week, go to God first rather than last. At the next moment of pressure, before you manage it, hide it or yield to it, speak one sentence to Him. And name your point of testing out loud to one trusted person before next Sabbath.

title: The Authority of His Word
kicker: Fifth Sabbath — Never Has a Man Spoken Like This
implication: Sequence 29 is Kaf (20) and Tet (9) — the open palm joined to the vessel of concealed good. Twenty-nine is the count of days in the shorter months, the number of a completed lunar cycle. The palm is what extends and offers; the Tet is what is carried inside it, hidden until it is opened. This is the shape of the Son's speech: ordinary words offered in an open hand, carrying an authority no one could see until it was released. They were amazed, because the container gave no warning of the contents.
theme: The first thing the crowds noticed about the Son was not His miracles but His speech: He taught as one having authority. Where the teachers of His day cited other teachers, He spoke as the source. For a congregation whose year is marked by the mouth, this is the governing service of the quarter. Authority in speech is the Son's possession, and any that we exercise is delegated, borrowed and accountable.

school.title: Not As the Scribes
school.text: The contrast is precise. The scribes transmitted authority; the Son carried it. Teach the difference between speaking under authority and speaking as though one had generated it. Every teacher in CMI stands in the first category, and confusing the two is how congregations are wounded.

school.title: The Words I Speak Are Spirit and Life
school.text: In John 6, when the crowd leaves, Peter answers with the only reason to stay: You have words of eternal life. Show that the Son's words are not merely accurate but life-giving — they do something rather than only describe something.

school.title: Only Say the Word
school.text: The centurion understood authority as a chain of command and recognised it in the Son, and the Son marked it as the greatest faith He had found (Matthew 8:8-10). Teach faith as the recognition of legitimate authority rather than as intensity of feeling.

school.title: The Tongue Is a Fire
school.text: James refuses to let the doctrine stay theoretical. The same mouth blesses and curses, and this ought not to be. Bring it home concretely — the reply you sent, the thing you said about someone in their absence, the word used to control a family member. In a house that celebrates the authority of the Son's word, careless speech is not a small sin.

communion: Before the elements, invite silence rather than more words. A Table set by the One whose word carries authority is not the place to add our own commentary; it is the place to receive what He said about the bread and the cup and let it stand.
bread: He said, take, eat. We do not improve on that sentence. We take the bread because He spoke, and His word does what it says.
cup: This cup is the new covenant in His blood. We take it as those who have heard words of eternal life and have nowhere else to go.
summons: This week, weigh your speech. Do not attach the Lord's authority to your preference — where you have said God told you and meant you decided, correct it to the person you said it to. And this week, keep one hard word unsaid for twenty-four hours before you say it.

title: The Son Who Serves
kicker: Sixth Sabbath — The Towel and the Basin
implication: Sequence 36 is Lamed (30) and Vav (6) — and the pairing is the most instructive in the quarter. The Lamed is the tallest letter in the alphabet, the only one that rises above the line of writing; the Vav is the nail, a single stroke descending from above. The highest letter joined to the descending stroke, on the Sabbath the Son lays aside His garments and kneels with a towel. Thirty-six is also twice eighteen, life doubled. What descends in this letter-pair does not diminish; it multiplies.
theme: On the night He was betrayed, knowing that the Father had given all things into His hands, the Son got up from supper and washed feet. John records the knowledge and the action in the same sentence, and the connection between them is the whole teaching. He did not serve because He had forgotten who He was. He served because He had not.

school.title: Knowing, He Got Up
school.text: Security is the precondition of service. The person who is uncertain of their standing cannot afford to take the low place, because they need the high one to prove something. Teach the congregation that servanthood is not self-erasure; it is what confidence looks like when it has nothing to defend.

school.title: Not So Among You
school.text: In Mark 10 the Son contrasts two systems: rulers of the nations lord it over people, but it shall not be so among you. Apply it to real structures — the household, the workplace, the church committee. Authority in the kingdom is measured by who it lifts, not by who it silences.

school.title: He Came to Give His Life a Ransom
school.text: The foot-washing is a parable of the cross performed with water. The Son's service is not merely a moral example of humility; it culminates in substitution — the Son of Man came to serve and to give His life a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Keep the two joined, or the passage becomes mere etiquette.

school.title: You Also Ought
school.text: The Son turns example into obligation. Close by making it concrete for CMI: name the specific act of service in this congregation that nobody wants and everybody benefits from, and let the leadership do it first this week, visibly and without announcement.

communion: Consider serving the elements today in a deliberately reversed order — leaders last, the newest and youngest first. Explain why before you begin, then let the practice preach rather than the explanation.
bread: He laid aside His garments and took a towel. We take the bread from the hands of a Lord who knelt, and we abandon every claim to be too senior for the low place.
cup: He gave His life a ransom for many. We take the cup as those served at infinite cost by One who owed us nothing.
summons: This week, take the low place once where it will not be noticed and cannot be repaid. And in the relationship where you currently hold the power, use it this week to lift the other person rather than to settle a point.

title: The Good Shepherd
kicker: Seventh Sabbath — He Lays Down His Life
implication: Sequence 43 is Mem (40) and Gimel (3). The Mem is water, the womb and the hidden depths — the letter drawn closed to conceal what it carries. The Gimel is the camel, the runner who carries provision across distance to those who cannot come and get it. A carrier and a hidden supply: the Shepherd who goes out over ground the sheep cannot cross, carrying what they cannot fetch, and who knows by name the ones He is carrying it to.
theme: The Son claims a title that carries both tenderness and authority. The good shepherd is not chiefly the one who comforts; He is the one who dies rather than run, and who knows His own by name. This is the middle Sabbath of the quarter, and the hinge of it: everything before has shown who He is, and everything after will follow Him to the cross and beyond it.

school.title: The Hired Hand Flees
school.text: The contrast in the passage is not between good and bad shepherds but between an owner and an employee. The hired hand leaves because the sheep are not his own. Teach the congregation to recognise the difference in those who lead them, and to recognise it in themselves wherever they carry responsibility for people.

school.title: I Know My Own
school.text: The knowledge is mutual and it is compared to the knowledge between the Father and the Son — the highest analogy available in the Gospel. Address the believer who feels generically saved but not personally known. The text will not permit that anonymity.

school.title: No One Takes It From Me
school.text: In John 10:18 the Son insists that no one takes His life; He lays it down of His own initiative. This governs how the cross must be preached in this house: not as a tragedy that happened to Him, but as an act He performed. He was not overpowered.

school.title: No One Will Snatch Them Out of My Hand
school.text: Close on the security of the sheep. The promise is not that the flock will never be attacked but that it cannot be seized. Distinguish carefully between assurance and presumption, and let the congregation hear that their grip on Him is not what holds — His grip on them is.

communion: Frame the Table as the Shepherd's provision for a flock He will not abandon. This is the meal of people who are known by name and cannot be taken.
bread: The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep. We take the bread as the flock He died rather than desert.
cup: No one will snatch them out of My hand. We take the cup with the assurance that our security rests on His grip and not on the strength of ours.
summons: This week, be an owner rather than a hired hand in one place where you have been going through the motions — a marriage, a team, a class, a person under your care. Stay where you have been preparing to leave, and say so to someone.

title: The Lamb Who Was Slain
kicker: Eighth Sabbath — Worthy Is the Lamb
implication: Sequence 50 is the Nun standing alone — the fish, the letter of faithfulness and of the soul that lives in waters it cannot see out of. Fifty is the number of release: the jubilee, the year in which debts are cancelled, property returns to its owner and the enslaved go free. On the Sabbath the congregation stands at the cross, the number over the day is the number of purchase and release. Nothing is remitted casually in a jubilee; every release is paid for by someone, and this one was paid in blood.
theme: The vision in Revelation 5 turns on a devastating substitution of images. John is told to look at the Lion; he turns and sees a Lamb standing, as if slain. What conquers in the kingdom does not look like what conquers anywhere else. This is the doctrinal centre of the quarter. Take the congregation to the cross without hurrying to the resurrection, and let the price stand in view.

school.title: Look, the Lion — Behold, a Lamb
school.text: John hears one thing and sees another, and the seeing corrects the hearing. Teach the congregation that the kingdom's power is cruciform, and that every attempt to build the church on a lion the world would recognise ends in something that is not the church.

school.title: Purchased With Blood
school.text: The verb is commercial. Peter presses it further: you were not redeemed with perishable things like silver or gold, but with precious blood (1 Peter 1:18-19). Ask the congregation what they habitually treat as more secure than that transaction, and why their sense of standing rises and falls with their performance if the purchase is complete.

school.title: Just and the Justifier
school.text: Romans 3:23-26 answers the question the cross exists to answer: how God can forgive without ceasing to be just. He did not waive the penalty; He bore it. Guard the congregation from a doctrine of grace that quietly implies God relaxed His standard.

school.title: From Every Tribe and Tongue
school.text: The purchase is international by design. Close on the scope: CMI's worship joins a company drawn from every people, and a congregation that celebrates this Lamb cannot maintain private categories of people it will not sit beside.

communion: Slow this Table down. Let there be a long silence between the bread and the cup, and resist filling it. Say only what is necessary: this is the price, and it has been paid in full.
bread: Worthy is the Lamb that was slain. We take the bread in the presence of a body that was broken and not spared.
cup: You purchased for God with Your blood men from every tribe and tongue and people and nation. We take the cup as the purchased, and we stop pricing ourselves by anything else.
summons: This week, live as the purchased. Where you have been trying to pay for a forgiveness already bought — through overwork, self-punishment or avoidance of God — stop the payment. And sit down this week with one person your instincts would keep at a distance.

title: The Firstborn From the Dead
implication: Sequence 57 is Nun (50) and Zayin (7) — the soul emerging from hidden waters joined to the crowned sword. The Nun is the letter of what comes up out of concealment; the Zayin is drawn as a Vav wearing a crown, the letter of completion and of the weapon that finishes rather than destroys. Emergence and coronation in one address, on the Sabbath of the resurrection. He did not merely come out. He came out crowned.
theme: The resurrection is not the happy ending of the Son's story; it is the beginning of ours. Paul calls Him the first fruits, which means the resurrection is a sample of a harvest rather than an exception to a rule. Teach it as an event in history with consequences in the body, not as a metaphor for renewal.

school.title: First Fruits, Not an Exception
school.text: A first portion implies the rest of the crop. Paul's argument is that the Son's resurrection guarantees a general one, and he stakes the credibility of the entire faith on it (1 Corinthians 15:14-19). Do not soften this. A Christianity that survives the loss of a bodily resurrection is not the one the apostles preached.

school.title: Buried With Him, Raised With Him
school.text: Romans 6 places the believer inside both events. Teach the practical consequence Paul draws: consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God. The reckoning is not a technique for feeling different; it is the recognition of a legal fact about your union with Him.

school.title: That I May Know Him
school.text: Philippians 3:10-11 orders the desire honestly — the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, in that sentence, from a man in prison. Warn against a resurrection theology that promises exemption from the sufferings the same verse names.

school.title: Set Your Mind on Things Above
school.text: Colossians 3:1-4 draws the conclusion: if you have been raised, seek what is above, for your life is hidden with Messiah in God. Close by asking what would visibly change in the congregation's week if the phrase your life is hidden with Him were treated as a fact about Monday.

communion: Set this Table as the meal of the living. Say clearly: we do not gather at a grave. The One we remember is not absent, and this bread is taken in the presence of a risen Lord.
bread: Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who are asleep. We take the bread as those joined to a body that death could not hold.
cup: We were buried with Him, and we walk in newness of life. We take the cup as people whose future is already secured in His past.
summons: This week, live from the resurrection rather than toward it. Name one thing you have treated as finally dead — a calling, a relationship, a hope — and refuse to bury it again without asking Him. Then reckon yourself dead to one specific sin, by name, and act on the reckoning.

title: Ascended and Enthroned
kicker: Tenth Sabbath — Seated at the Right Hand
implication: Sequence 64 is Samech (60) and Dalet (4). The Samech is the closed circle — the letter of support, of what surrounds and upholds without a gap; the Dalet is the door. A circle with a door in it is the exact picture of this Sabbath's doctrine: authority that encompasses everything, with an opening cut into it for the people it governs on behalf of. He is far above all rule and authority, and He is given as head over all things to the church.
theme: The Son did not conclude His work by returning to obscurity. He ascended, and He is seated — a posture that says the work is finished — and He is seated in authority over everything that concerns His people. The ascension is the most neglected article of the faith in most congregations, and its neglect leaves believers with a Saviour who saved them and a world that now runs itself. Correct that this Sabbath.

school.title: He Sat Down
school.text: Hebrews 10:12-14 makes the posture the point: having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, He sat down. The priests of the old order stood, because their work was never finished. Teach the congregation to read the seated Son as the end of religious striving.

school.title: Far Above All Rule and Authority
school.text: Paul's list is deliberately exhaustive — every rule, authority, power, dominion and name. Apply it to the powers the congregation actually fears: economic, political, spiritual, medical, familial. None of them is unranked, and none of them outranks Him.

school.title: Given as Head Over All Things to the Church
school.text: Note the direction of the gift. The Son is not merely head of the church; He is given as head over all things to the church. His universal authority is exercised for the benefit of His body. This is the answer to the question of why a sovereign Lord permits what He permits — He governs everything on behalf of His people, even where we cannot yet trace it.

school.title: Why Do You Stand Looking Into the Sky?
school.text: The angels' question at the ascension is a rebuke to spectator faith (Acts 1:11), and the promise of the Spirit in Acts 1:8 is the answer. Close on the commission: the ascended Lord did not leave His people watching the sky but working the earth with power given for witness.

communion: Frame this Table as the meal of a people whose Lord is enthroned. He is not absent and He is not idle; He is seated, and He presides over this Table from the throne.
bread: He offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, and sat down. We take the bread as those with nothing left to add to a finished work.
cup: He is head over all things for the sake of His body. We take the cup under a government we cannot see and can trust.
summons: This week, name the power you are actually afraid of — the market, the diagnosis, the office, the family member — and place it under His feet out loud. Then stop watching the sky: take one concrete action this week that assumes His authority is real.

title: Our Great High Priest
kicker: Eleventh Sabbath — He Always Lives to Intercede
implication: Sequence 71 is Ayin (70) and Aleph (1). The Ayin is the eye and also the spring — sight and source in one letter; the Aleph is unity, the One. Seventy-one is a prime number, indivisible. The eye that never closes, joined to the One who cannot be divided or replaced: a priesthood that does not change hands, held by One who always lives, watching continuously over people who are frequently unaware they are being watched over.
theme: The Son's work did not end at the ascension; it changed office. He lives to intercede, and He does so continuously, for the people He has already saved. This is the Sabbath for the congregation's weary — those who assume they have exhausted God's patience and have quietly stopped asking.

school.title: A Priesthood That Does Not Change Hands
school.text: The argument of Hebrews 7 turns on mortality: former priests died and were replaced, but He continues forever. Teach the congregation what permanence means for their assurance — the One representing them will not be succeeded, retired or removed.

school.title: He Always Lives to Intercede
school.text: The present participle describes unbroken activity. While you slept, while you failed, while you were not thinking of Him, He was praying for you. Set Luke 22:31-32 beside it: I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail — spoken to Peter before the denial, not after it.

school.title: Who Is the One Who Condemns?
school.text: Romans 8:33-34 sets accusation against intercession and asks who will bring a charge. The answer is that the only qualified Judge is the One who died, was raised, is at the right hand and is interceding. Teach the congregation to test the voice of accusation by its source.

school.title: If Anyone Sins, We Have an Advocate
school.text: John writes so that we may not sin, and then tells us what to do when we do (1 John 2:1-2). Close pastorally: the provision for failure is not a licence for it, and the believer who cannot receive the advocacy will either despair or pretend. Neither produces holiness.

communion: Bring the discouraged to this Table first. Say to the congregation: you are not here to persuade Him to take your side. He has been praying for you all week, and this meal is His invitation, not your appeal.
bread: He is able to save forever those who draw near to God through Him. We take the bread as the permanently represented.
cup: He always lives to make intercession. We take the cup as those whose Advocate has never once been unavailable, and whose accuser has no standing in this court.
summons: This week, come back sooner. Cut the delay between your failure and your return to God from days to minutes. And take up intercession yourself: pray daily by name this week for one person who does not know you are doing it.

title: The Head of the Body
kicker: Twelfth Sabbath — Joined and Held Together
implication: Sequence 78 is Ayin (70) and Chet (8) — the eye joined to the fence. Seventy-eight is six times thirteen, and thirteen is the value of both echad, one, and ahavah, love. A body that sees, held together within an enclosure, growing by love into one. Every element of this Sabbath's teaching is in the letters: perception of one another, connection that holds, and the oneness that love produces rather than uniformity imposes.
theme: Everything the quarter has taught about the Son now lands on the congregation itself. He is the head, and CMI is a body — not an audience, not a service provider, not a network of individuals with a shared preference. Teach this as the practical outcome of the whole quarter, because a Christology that never becomes ecclesiology stays theoretical.

school.title: He Is the Head, in Everything Preeminent
school.text: Colossians 1:18 gives the Son first place in the body as He has first place in creation. Address the congregation's habit of organising church life around gifted individuals: any body arranged around a member rather than the Head is describing a tumour, not growth.

school.title: What Every Joint Supplies
school.text: Paul's picture is of a body held together by connections — joints, not merely parts. The growth comes from what the connections supply. Apply it to attendance and relationship: a member who is present but unjoined contributes nothing to what this text describes.

school.title: The Parts You Would Not Choose
school.text: In 1 Corinthians 12 the members that seem weaker are declared necessary, and those we consider less honourable receive greater honour. Confront the congregation's informal hierarchy — who gets consulted, who gets thanked, who is invisible in this house.

school.title: Speaking the Truth in Love
school.text: The phrase is the mechanism of the growth, not a decoration on it. Truth without love wounds; love without truth stalls; together they mature a body. Close with a specific charge: name a form of honest speech CMI needs to recover, and a form of cruelty done in truth's name that must stop.

communion: Take this Table with attention to the people beside you. Ask the congregation to look up rather than close their eyes, and to receive the elements as one body before receiving them as individuals.
bread: We who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread. We take it together, and we refuse to eat as strangers.
cup: From Him the whole body is fitted and held together. We take the cup as members joined to a Head and to each other.
summons: This week, supply what your joint supplies. Do the one thing in this body that you can do and have been leaving to someone else. And restore one connection here that has quietly gone cold — make contact before next Sabbath.

title: The Son Who Is Coming
kicker: Thirteenth Sabbath — Closing the Quarter in Expectation
implication: Sequence 85 is Pe (80) and Hei (5) — and it closes the quarter on the year's own governing letter. The Hebrew year 5787 resolves to Pe (80) and Zayin (7): the mouth given an edge and a crown. Here the Pe appears joined not to the sword but to the Hei, the window, the letter of breath and revelation — the opening left in a wall so that what is enclosed is never sealed. The quarter began on the silent Aleph; it ends on the mouth and the window. Behold, I am coming quickly is the sentence, and the window is how it reaches us.
theme: The quarter closes where the New Testament closes: with a promise of return and a congregation answering it. Everything taught since September has been about who He is; this final Sabbath is about what we are waiting for. Teach expectation as a discipline rather than a mood. The congregation is not asked to speculate about timing but to live in a particular way because of a certainty.

school.title: Grace That Instructs
school.text: Titus ties the appearing of grace to a curriculum: it instructs us to deny and to live. Teach against the two errors in the room — those who hear grace as permission and those who hear instruction as merit. The same grace that saves also trains.

school.title: In the Present Age
school.text: The waiting is done here, sensibly and righteously, in the ordinary present. Expectation that produces withdrawal from work, family or civic responsibility has misread the text. Show that hope in the New Testament always produces engagement, never evacuation.

school.title: Everyone Who Has This Hope Purifies Himself
school.text: 1 John 3:2-3 gives the ethical consequence of the return: we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is — and everyone who has this hope purifies himself. The motive for holiness here is resemblance to a Person we are about to see, not fear of a penalty.

school.title: The Spirit and the Bride Say Come
school.text: Close the quarter on Revelation 22:17 and 20. The last movement of scripture is an invitation extended outward and a prayer offered upward. Let CMI end this quarter doing both: inviting whoever is thirsty, and answering the promise with Amen, come, Lord Jesus.

communion: This is the quarter's final Table, and the most forward-looking. Remind the congregation of what the meal itself declares: as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes. The Table has an expiry date, and it is His return.
bread: We take the bread proclaiming His death until He comes — a meal that will one day be unnecessary because the One it remembers will be at the table in person.
cup: Behold, I am coming quickly. We take the cup as those who answer that sentence rather than merely hear it: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.
summons: Go into this week and into the coming quarter as people expecting Him. Order one thing in your life this week that you would not want to be found doing, and start one thing you would want to be found doing. Then extend the invitation: speak to one person this month who is thirsty, and say come.
